newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan plans free port for Central Asian oil, gas.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan plans free port for Central Asian oil, gas.

text.p: Pakistan, dependent on imported fuel to meet rising domestic demand, plans to develop a free port to process oil and gas from Central Asia, a leading member of the government said on Tuesday.

"We are ready to build a massive infrastructure in Gwadar to create a free petroleum port facility to develop whatever processing is required of oil and gas resources from Central Asia," former finance minister Sartaj Aziz told an industry conference.
Aziz, tipped to regain his old post when prime minister Nawaz Sharif names his cabinet, said that Gwadar, in the thinly-populated southern province of Balochistan, was an ideal location.
He said Gwadar was 1,300 km (812 miles) from gas fields in Turkmenistan and 2,500 km (1,563 miles) from Kazakh oil fields.
Official projections show demand in Pakistan for refined oil products rising to 26.9 million tonnes a year by 2000 from a current 14.3 million.

Pakistan, which imports 60 percent of its crude oil and 62 percent of its oil products requirements, imported oil and products worth $1.9 billion in 1995/96 (July-June), or 17 percent of its total import bill.
It has shown interest in importing gas by pipeline from Iran, Qatar or Turkmenistan, but pricing and other problems associated with each project have yet to be resolved.
Oil and gas pipelines from Turkmenistan, which could be built for an estimated 4.5 billion, would have to pass through Afghanistan, where war has raged for 17 years.

"Hopefully the situation in Afghanistan will also improve in the near future to permit this oil and gas to come, not only for Pakistan's needs, but also for exports to all the regions which are east of Gwadar," Aziz said.
President Farooq Leghari told the conference gas imports could become more profitable and economical if countries in the region cooperated in building pipelines.

"A large gas market in Pakistan and neighbouring countries creates attractive opportunities for regional projects leading to a win-win situation for gas producers, pipeline sponsors and end-users," Leghari said.
He said Pakistan had potential reserves far in excess of its proven reserves of half a billion barrels of oil and 30 trillion cubic feet of gas, but needed huge investment in exploration.
Gulfaraz Ahmad, secretary at the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Resources, said Pakistan wanted to achieve the lowest landed price for imported gas and early delivery.

"Thus for us, cost is the king and time is of the essence. When we talk about imports of natural gas, we favour regionally optimised arrangements, lowest-cost pipelines exploiting optimal routes, economy of scale and flexibility of offtakes," he said.
